Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (CTO), Priya Nair (Lead ML Eng), Ben Torres (Platform Eng), Aisha Rahman (Privacy)
Agenda: quick onboarding to Hosted Gen chat, streaming behavior, param tuning, retries/ids, Console + Optimize suggestions, next steps and pilot scoping

Auto-summary (auto-generated, short):
- Demo of hosted chat generation with streaming and parameter knobs.
- Discussed tokenization, seq length distribution, KV caching and cost/latency trade-offs.
- Agreed to run a benchmark and share SOC2 + network diagram.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight. I'm Maya, on the AE side, with Ravi, our systems engineer. Quick intro from you Daniel?
[00:12] Daniel: Yeah hi, Daniel Kim, CTO at Orion. We're looking to add summarization and chat to our clinical notes product. Main concerns are PII handling, latency under 300ms median and predictable spend.
[00:22] Ravi: Great, thanks. Quick note, we'll demo the hosted API path first — low friction — then show Console Optimize suggestions for batching and caching. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:35] Priya: quick one — we do most of our inference in a VPC today, is hosted compatible? Like we need private traffic and audit logs.
[00:45] Maya: yes, hosted supports private peering options and detailed audit logs; we'll send the network diagram. Also SOC2 and ISO are available in the doc pack.

[03:10] (screen share starts)
[03:20] Ravi: Ok share screen, console home. First, the simplest call — a streaming chat generation. We set model=model-open-7B-q4 (example), stream=true, and you get tokens as they're produced. Two big knobs: max_tokens and stop sequences, plus temperature/top_p.
[03:55] Ben: How does streaming affect latency numbers vs non-stream?
[04:02] Ravi: Streaming reduces perceived latency because partial tokens arrive earlier; total end-to-end might be same, but perceived TTF (time-to-first-byte) often much lower. For small responses streaming wins. For very long outputs batching matters.

[06:30] Maya: A note on cost: tokens billed per output and input — so shorter outputs + stop sequences = cost control. Also Optimize tab will suggest trim prompts or use summarizer models.

[08:05] Priya: We saw reference to K-V cache in the docs — we want to know about session memory across turns.
[08:15] Ravi: Right, Redwood maintains KV cache for decoder-only flows; it's the K-V cash — sometimes transcripts show as 'K V cash' — but basically reuse previous key/values to speed up subsequent tokens. With streaming we still maintain KV live; for long conversation you want to manage prefix lengths or use prefix caching options in console.

[12:00] Daniel: Our app has many short queries — summarize one paragraph, answer a question. Will batching help?
[12:10] Ravi: Batching is workload-dependent. For many short, concurrent requests batching increases throughput and lowers cost per token but can add tail latency. Console Optimize will recommend a batching profile: max batch size with a latency SLO. For your 300ms median, we might keep small batch sizes and rely on autoscale.

[15:25] Maya: quick demo of retries — we recommend idempotency keys for POSTs. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Example: client retries at 200ms, 500ms, 1200ms with jitter. Avoid hammering during an outage; Redwood auto-fallbacks to a cheaper variant before returning error if configured.

[18:40] Priya: What about partial failures — mid-stream disconnects?
[18:47] Ravi: If a stream disconnects you can resume from last committed token if you're storing the prefix; otherwise client retries should be idempotent. We surface streaming session status in the console and in trace logs, so you can debug where the break happened.

[21:00] Ben: Security — what about keys and rotation?
[21:05] Maya: Keys can be rotated via Console and we support KMS integration for payload encryption at rest. Aisha, do you want audit log specifics?
[21:15] Aisha: yes we need retention windows and field-level redaction options.
[21:20] Maya: We'll attach the compliance packet; retention and redact options vary by plan but are available in Dedicated and Private.

[25:40] (Ravi switches to API examples)
[25:50] Ravi: Example payload: POST /v1/chat/generate with messages: system+user; set temperature=0.2 for deterministic summaries, top_p=0.9 for variation control. If you want safety, use temperature 0 and a reranking pass.
[26:20] Priya: reranking pass — cost tradeoff?
[26:24] Ravi: Yes, reranking doubles compute roughly (one pass to generate N candidates, then a cheap scorer). Optimize can recommend a single-model rerank vs two-model architecture based on your quality metrics.

[29:30] Maya: Console tour — on the model card we show throughput curves, token cost estimates, and recommended quantization for your workload — e.g., q4_0 for latency-focused, q8_1 for better perf/cost in some cases (note: pronouncing quantization sometimes comes out weird — 'quantz' in the transcript).

[31:45] Daniel: For pilot success criteria, we want <300ms median and <5% unacceptable hallucinations on 2k eval prompts. Can Redwood help with eval harness?
[31:58] Ravi: Absolutely. We have an evals module and can run your prompt set to produce quality/latency/cost tradeoffs; Optimize will also flag regression alerts.

[34:10] (brief cross-talk)
[34:22] Ben: Any known limits on tokens per request? We have occasionally 6k token docs.
[34:30] Ravi: Hosted supports up to 16k tokens depending on model variant; practical limits depend on memory and kernel selection. For very long docs we recommend chunk-and-summarize — console has a chunking helper.

[37:00] Priya: Useful — what about region routing? We have EU data residency needs.
[37:08] Maya: You can pin region, and Dedicated/Private give stronger residency guarantees. We'll include region-specific SLAs.

[39:10] Daniel: latency SLOs — how predictable is the hosted path under bursty load?
[39:18] Ravi: Predictability is handled via prioritized routing and dedicated pools. For bursty but not mission-critical you can use hosted with autoscale; for strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated pools. Also cloud-side autoscaling + burst capacity can be configured in Console.

[42:05] Maya: Recap of next steps — we'll send SOC2/network diagram, pricing and pilot template; Ravi will run a bench using Priya's sample workload when she shares seq length distribution.

[44:30] Priya: timeline-wise we aim to start pilot mid-September, 3-week pilot.
[44:40] Maya: sounds good. Any final quick questions?
[44:48] Aisha: just confirm audit log retention for audits — we'll review the packet.
[45:00] Maya: will do. Thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and link to shared drive.
[45:12] (meeting ends)

References and links mentioned: Console model cards, SOC2 pack (link sent post-call), sample bench template (Ravi to share), pilot scope doc.
